context: Thandi buys a fridge on hire purchase. She pays no deposit, the whole cash price is repaid over a whole number of years with simple interest, and a fixed insurance premium is added to every monthly payment.

params.why: the monthly repayment must not fall exactly on a half cent, so rounding to the nearest cent is unambiguous
keeps the insurance premium realistically small next to the monthly repayment (at most half of it)

stem: Thandi buys a fridge on hire purchase. The cash price of the fridge is $\text{R{=cash}}$. She pays no deposit and pays the fridge off over ${=yrs}$ years at an interest rate of ${=r}\%$ p.a., charged as simple interest. An insurance premium of $\text{R{=prem_t}}$ is added to every monthly payment. Calculate Thandi's monthly payment in rand, correct to the nearest cent.
solution: There is no deposit, so the amount financed is the cash price: $P = \text{R{=cash}}$. The interest rate is $i = {=i_t}$ and the period is $n = {=yrs}$ years.
Calculate the accumulated amount: $A = P(1 + in) = {=cash}(1 + {=i_t} \times {=yrs}) = \text{R{=acc_t}}$.
The agreement runs for ${=yrs} \times 12 = {=m}$ months, so the monthly repayment on the hire purchase agreement is $\frac{{=acc_t}}{{=m}} = \text{R{=inst_t}}$ (to the nearest cent).
Add the insurance premium to the monthly repayment: $\text{R{=inst_t}} + \text{R{=prem_t}} = \text{R{=tot_t}}$.
notes: Entry point of the skill: the book's we08 method (A = P(1 + in), divide by the number of months, add the premium) with the deposit removed and the term a whole number of years, so n needs no conversion from months. Simple interest is stated in the stem so a blind solver cannot reach for compound interest; the book leaves it implicit. Cash price is a multiple of R100 so A is a whole number of rand. Premium is in 5-cent steps (R10.00 to R35.00) and is kept at no more than half the monthly repayment. Tie check keeps the repayment off an exact half cent; because the premium is an exact number of cents, rounding the repayment first (as the book does) and rounding the sum give the same answer. I checked 20 000 sampled instances against an independent step-by-step calculation that rounds as the book does: they agree, about 99.5% of draws are accepted, and answers run from about R57 to R560. Typical errors to watch for in review or blind solves: adding the premium once instead of to every month, dividing by the number of years instead of months, using compound interest. No misconceptions are catalogued for this objective and a numeric family has no distractors to tag, so none are proposed.
